_readme: Base image knowledge shared by the backend rule engine and the VS Code extension.
sizeMb figures are uncompressed `docker images` sizes for linux/amd64, rounded. They
are estimates used to rank suggestions and to show a user roughly what a swap buys
them - never presented as measured facts. Re-measure before editing.
compatibility is how likely the swap is to be drop-in, as a percentage:
100  identical libc and toolchain, no expected behaviour change
95+  same distro family, may lack a package you install explicitly
80-94 different libc (musl) - native addons may need rebuilding
<80  no shell or package manager (distroless), or a different runtime layout
The VS Code completion provider offers `tags` for the matching family, so the ordering
within recommendations is the ordering the user sees.

recommendations.note: Alpine uses musl libc. Packages with native addons (sharp, bcrypt, canvas) may need rebuilding or a -slim base instead. Pinned to a minor version so the floating-tag rule passes too — bump it deliberately.
Same image, but 22.x moves under you as patches ship.
Tracks the current LTS line. Convenient, but the major version moves under you.
Debian-based, so glibc native modules keep working. The safe first move off a full image.
No shell and no package manager, so nothing to exploit and nothing to debug with. Final stage of a multi-stage build only.
Debian-based. Wheels for most packages install without a compiler, unlike Alpine.
Smallest, but manylinux wheels do not apply - numpy, pandas and friends compile from source, which can make builds far slower and images larger than -slim.
Final stage only. No pip, no shell.
Near-identical package set via apt, smaller, and patched on a predictable cadence.
Dramatically smaller, but apk package names differ and musl replaces glibc.
For a statically or near-statically linked binary. No shell, no apt.
Same distro with the docs and locale data stripped. Almost always a free win.
Final stage of a multi-stage build, for a compiled binary.
Build with CGO_ENABLED=0 in a golang builder stage, then copy the binary here. A Go service rarely needs anything else.
For the builder stage. Requires build-base if you use cgo.
When you need a shell alongside the binary for debugging or an entrypoint script.
A JRE is enough to run a built jar; the JDK is only needed to compile it. openjdk: images are deprecated in favour of temurin.
Debian-based JRE. Use when a native library needs glibc.
Same configuration and module set for static-file serving and reverse proxying.
Gems with native extensions still build, unlike on Alpine.
Needs build-base for native gems, which often cancels out the saving.
Use with docker-php-ext-install for the extensions you actually need.
For workers and CLI tooling rather than a web SAPI.
Runtime only. Build with the sdk image in a separate stage.
For a self-contained or AOT-published binary.
